lesson.title: What's Inside? Finding Percent Composition
lesson.summary: Percent composition reports what fraction of a compound's total mass comes from each element, using molar mass and mole calculations to turn a chemical formula into a mass breakdown.
lesson.body:
Two very different compounds can share some of the same elements, but a chemist often needs to know, by mass, how much of a sample is actually made of a particular element. Percent composition answers exactly that question. It is the percentage of the total mass of a compound that is contributed by each individual element in its formula, and it is calculated directly from the molar mass work and mole calculations already established for the compound.

The general approach is to first find the molar mass of the whole compound, then find the mass contributed by each element within one mole of that compound, and finally divide each element's contribution by the total molar mass and multiply by 100 to get a percentage. In formula form, percent by mass of an element equals the mass of that element in one mole of the compound, divided by the molar mass of the compound, times 100 percent. Because this calculation depends entirely on having an accurate molar mass, it could not be done without the molar mass skills built up earlier.

Glucose, C6H12O6, is a useful worked example because its composition is well known and easy to check. Its molar mass is calculated by adding the contributions of each element: 6 carbon atoms contribute 6 x 12.01 = 72.06 g/mol, 12 hydrogen atoms contribute 12 x 1.008 = 12.096 g/mol, and 6 oxygen atoms contribute 6 x 16.00 = 96.00 g/mol, for a total molar mass of 72.06 + 12.096 + 96.00 = 180.16 g/mol. The percent composition of carbon is then 72.06 / 180.16 x 100 = 40.00 percent. The percent composition of hydrogen is 12.096 / 180.16 x 100 = 6.71 percent. The percent composition of oxygen is 96.00 / 180.16 x 100 = 53.29 percent. Adding these three percentages gives 40.00 + 6.71 + 53.29 = 100.00 percent, which is exactly the check a chemist should always perform, since the percentages of all elements in a compound must sum to 100.

Percent composition is useful on its own for practical questions, such as figuring out how much nitrogen by mass is available in a fertilizer compound, or how much iron by mass is present in an ore like hematite, Fe2O3. But its deeper importance is that it runs the mole calculation process in reverse. Instead of starting from a known formula and predicting a mass breakdown, a chemist can start from an experimentally measured mass breakdown, the percent composition of an unknown compound, and use it to work backward toward the compound's formula.

That reverse process is exactly what comes next: using percent composition data as the starting point for determining a compound's empirical formula. Every percent composition calculation is, in effect, a rehearsal for that skill, since it requires the same fluency in converting between mass, molar mass, and moles, just applied in the forward direction first so the reverse direction makes sense afterward.
